In addition to the FOMC’s hawkish stance (75 bp hike to 3–3.25% and ongoing QT), the July 2022 SLOOS points to a procyclical tightening in bank credit that likely amplifies the contractionary impulse. Banks reported tighter standards and terms for C&I loans across firm sizes, CRE, most residential mortgage categories (including GSE-eligible and jumbo), HELOCs, credit cards, and subprime auto; they also raised loan pricing and collateral requirements. Banks cited a weaker economic outlook, industry-specific stresses, and liquidity concerns. Demand softened in CRE, while C&I and HELOC demand strengthened—consistent with precautionary or working-capital needs rather than expansionary intent. Net effect: tighter bank lending conditions add to higher policy rates, weighing on capex, housing, and consumer credit. While core bank resilience (capital/liquidity) buffers tail risks, SLOOS tilts the near-term growth/risk-asset outlook more negatively than a policy-only read. Adjusting for SLOOS, sentiment is modestly more negative than the prior FSR-based read.
